sections.title: Peptic ulcer: causes, pathogenesis & risk factors

blocks.text: A **peptic ulcer** is a breach that goes **through the muscularis mucosae** in mucosa exposed to acid–pepsin: stomach and duodenum mostly, but also the lower oesophagus, the jejunum beside a gastric anastomosis, or the ileum next to a Meckel’s diverticulum. An **erosion** stays above the muscularis mucosae. An **acute** ulcer shows no fibrosis; a **chronic** one does.

blocks.title: Helicobacter pylori: what makes it ulcerogenic
items: Gram-negative, spiral, flagellated rod that lives under the mucus layer on gastric epithelium
Sticks to the **Lewis b antigen** via the **BabA** adhesin
**Urease** turns urea into ammonia, creating a buffered micro-environment against acid
Colonises **only gastric-type epithelium**; it reaches the duodenum only where there are patches of **gastric metaplasia**
Virulence: **CagA** (injected into epithelial cells) and **VacA** (pore-forming toxin) strains cause more disease
Usually acquired in childhood (oral–oral or faecal–oral); most carriers never develop disease

blocks.title: Duodenal versus gastric ulcer
rows: About 70% (most of the rest are NSAID-related)
Too much acid: antral-predominant gastritis drives acid hypersecretion
Weak mucosal defence (H. pylori + NSAIDs + smoking); acid normal or low
First part of duodenum (cap); Davidson: half on the anterior wall
Usually single; 90% on the lesser curve in the antrum or at the body–antrum junction

blocks.title: How antral H. pylori gastritis leads to a duodenal ulcer (Fig. 21.36)
items: 1. Antral gastritis depletes **somatostatin** from D cells
2. Loss of this brake lets G cells release more **gastrin**
3. Gastrin drives **acid hypersecretion** by parietal cells
4. The extra acid reaching the duodenum induces **gastric metaplasia** there
5. H. pylori colonises the metaplastic patches → duodenitis → **ulcer**
Contrast: **corpus-predominant** gastritis → atrophy and hypochlorhydria → gastric ulcer and **gastric cancer** risk (commoner in East Asia)

blocks.title: NSAIDs, aspirin and rarer causes
items: NSAIDs and aspirin block **cyclo-oxygenase**, so the mucosa loses protective prostaglandins
COX-2-selective drugs cause less gastric damage (but not none); cardiovascular risk limits their use
About **30%** of regular NSAID users have an ulcer at endoscopy, yet only **1–2%** bleed or perforate
H. pylori and NSAIDs are **independent and synergistic**: odds ratio about **61** for ulcer when both are present, compared with neither
Rarer causes: **Zollinger–Ellison syndrome**, hyperparathyroidism, vascular insufficiency, sarcoidosis, Crohn’s disease

blocks.title: Risk factors for peptic ulcer
rows: One of the two most important risks for NSAID ulcer (Box 24.31)
The other most important NSAID-ulcer risk
Past NSAID adverse event; high-dose or several NSAIDs; high-risk NSAID
Steroids alone barely change bleeding risk (RR 1.1–1.5) but **synergise** with NSAIDs
Do not cause ulcers but make any bleed worse
Raises GU risk more than DU risk; ulcers heal less and complicate more
Prevalence 0.1–0.2%, falling in the West with eradication, high in developing countries

blocks.text: **Zollinger–Ellison syndrome** = severe peptic ulceration + gastric acid hypersecretion + a **gastrin-secreting neuro-endocrine tumour** (gastrinoma) of pancreas or duodenum. About **0.1%** of duodenal ulcers; **20–60%** have **MEN 1**. Ulcers are often **multiple and in odd places** (post-bulbar duodenum, jejunum, oesophagus), respond poorly to standard therapy, and **diarrhoea** is common because the acid flood inactivates pancreatic lipase.
Two causes dominate: **H. pylori** and **NSAIDs/aspirin**. An apparently “idiopathic” ulcer is usually a missed H. pylori infection or hidden NSAID use; gastrinoma explains under 1%.

Books disagree on numbers. Davidson: about **90%** of DU patients carry H. pylori; Kumar: now **50–75%** in the developed world and falling. Davidson puts half of DUs on the **anterior** wall; Step-Up says most are on the **posterior** wall. In exams, follow Davidson.

Diet and stress: Zero to Finals lists stress, caffeine and spicy food as acid-raising ulcer factors, but Step-Up states that stress and diet (coffee, spice) have **not** been shown to raise ulcer risk, and Davidson says moderate alcohol is harmless and no special diet is needed.

blocks.note: Look at: H. pylori on gastric mucosa (modified Giemsa stain) and the spiral bacterium on scanning electron microscopy.

sections.title: GORD: mechanisms, risk factors & hiatus hernia

blocks.text: Brief reflux is normal and is cleared by peristalsis and neutralised by alkaline saliva. **GORD** is the result of **prolonged** contact between refluxed gastroduodenal juice and the oesophageal lining, producing symptoms and sometimes oesophagitis. The oesophagus has a **squamous** lining, which tolerates acid far worse than gastric columnar mucosa. Reflux heartburn affects about **30%** of the population (Davidson).

blocks.title: Why reflux happens (Fig. 21.26)
rows: Either low basal tone, or normal tone with frequent inappropriate relaxations
Occur without a swallow, often after meals; cause almost all reflux in healthy people and about **two-thirds** in GORD
Loses the abdominal–thoracic pressure gradient that pinches the hiatus and the oblique cardio-oesophageal angle
Defective peristalsis; persists after oesophagitis heals, so it is a primary defect
Acid is the main irritant; pepsin and bile add injury
Unbuffered acid layer in the proximal stomach after meals acts as a reservoir, especially with a hernia

blocks.title: Risk factors for GORD
items: **Obesity** and **pregnancy** (raised abdominal pressure)
Dietary items that relax the LOS: **fat, chocolate, alcohol, coffee/tea**; large meals
**Smoking**
Drugs: **antimuscarinics, calcium-channel blockers, nitrates**, tricyclics
**Systemic sclerosis**; previous treatment for achalasia
**Hiatus hernia** (but reflux also occurs without one)
Prevalence rises with age

blocks.title: Hiatus hernia: sliding versus rolling
rows: Gastro-oesophageal junction and part of the stomach slide up above the diaphragm
Fundus rolls up through the hiatus beside the oesophagus; the junction stays below the diaphragm
Incompetent, so symptoms come from reflux
The common type; hiatus hernia is present in about 30% of over-50s, often silent

blocks.note: Look at: rolling (para-oesophageal) versus sliding hernia diagrams, with barium meals showing an intrathoracic stomach and a gastric volvulus.

blocks.text: Almost every patient with **oesophagitis, Barrett’s or a peptic stricture** has a hiatus hernia, yet hernias are very common in people with no symptoms and some symptomatic patients have none.

sections.title: Clinical presentations of PUD and GORD

blocks.title: Peptic ulcer disease
items: Recurrent **epigastric** pain with three features: epigastric site, link to food, and **episodic** pattern; relapses and remissions over decades
Patient **points with one finger** to the epigastrium: strongly suggests ulcer
DU pain is classically **nocturnal** and worse when **hungry** (not reliable); pain of both GU and DU may ease with antacids
Classic exam teaching: **eating worsens GU pain and eases DU pain**
Occasional vomiting in about 40%; **daily persistent vomiting** suggests gastric outlet obstruction
Anorexia and weight loss are more typical of GU
**Back pain** suggests a penetrating posterior ulcer
May present with haematemesis, coffee-ground vomit, melaena or iron-deficiency anaemia

blocks.text: Symptoms predict an ulcer poorly. In about a third the story is atypical, especially in the **elderly** and **NSAID users**: the ulcer may be silent until it presents with **anaemia, haematemesis or perforation**.

blocks.title: GORD
items: **Heartburn** and **regurgitation**, brought on by bending, straining or lying flat, often after meals
**Waterbrash**: reflex salivation as acid enters the gullet
Woken at night by **choking**; odynophagia or dysphagia
**Atypical chest pain** that can mimic angina
Extra-oesophageal: hoarseness (“acid laryngitis”), chronic cough, asthma, recurrent chest infections, dental erosions
Up to half present with something other than classic heartburn

blocks.title: Reflux pain versus cardiac ischaemic pain
rows: Radiates to neck or left arm

blocks.title: Alarm features in dyspepsia (Box 21.15)
items: Unintended weight loss
Anaemia
Vomiting
Haematemesis or melaena
Dysphagia
A mass felt in the abdomen
Plus: **new dyspepsia over 55** needs investigation

blocks.text: In GORD, the severity of heartburn tells you little about the severity of oesophagitis. With chest pain, **exclude a cardiac cause first**. A good PPI response supports GORD, but no response does not exclude it.

blocks.alt: Dyspepsia algorithm: alarm features or new symptoms over 55 lead to urgent endoscopy; otherwise test non-invasively for H. pylori, eradicate if positive and scope if symptoms persist; heartburn-predominant symptoms are managed as GORD.

blocks.title: Endoscopy in suspected peptic ulcer
items: **Endoscopy (OGD)** is the investigation of choice and allows biopsy for H. pylori and cancer
Every **gastric ulcer is biopsied** (several samples from rim and base): benign and malignant ulcers can look alike
Repeat endoscopy to confirm a GU has **healed** (Kumar: at about 6 weeks)
Barium studies miss small ulcers and erosions
Under 55 with ulcer-type symptoms and no alarm features: non-invasive H. pylori testing instead of endoscopy

blocks.note: Look at: a clean-based duodenal ulcer with no stigmata of recent haemorrhage.

blocks.title: Tests for H. pylori (Box 21.34)
rows: Cannot tell past from current infection; stays positive after cure, so useless for checking eradication
High sensitivity and specificity; used to diagnose and to confirm eradication
Bacterial urease makes ammonia, pH rises, colour changes; > 95% specific, about 85% sensitive
Specific but false negatives; takes days
“Gold standard”; gives antibiotic sensitivities but slow and insensitive

blocks.text: PPIs and antibiotics cause **false negatives**: stop PPIs **2 weeks** and antibiotics **4 weeks** before a breath or stool test (H2-receptor antagonists may continue).

blocks.title: Investigating GORD
items: Young patient, typical symptoms, no alarm features: treat **empirically** without tests
**Endoscopy** is the test of choice if over 50–55, atypical symptoms or a complication is suspected; a **normal endoscopy does not exclude GORD**
**24-hour pH monitoring**: diagnostic if pH is **< 4 for more than 6–7%** of the recording; used when the diagnosis is unclear and **before anti-reflux surgery**
Kumar reports a composite **DeMeester score > 14.72** as abnormal; a wireless (Bravo) capsule avoids a nasal tube
**Impedance** detects weakly acidic or alkaline reflux missed by pH testing
Barium only shows complications; manometry if a motility disorder is suspected

blocks.title: Los Angeles grading of oesophagitis (Fig. 32.11)
rows: Mucosal break(s) within the folds, each ≤ 5 mm
At least one break > 5 mm, not continuous between two folds
Breaks continuous between the tops of folds, but not circumferential

blocks.title: Suspected Zollinger–Ellison syndrome
items: **Fasting serum gastrin** off acid suppression: grossly raised (10- to 1000-fold)
**Secretin test**: normally gastrin falls or stays the same; in gastrinoma it **rises paradoxically**
Localise and stage with **CT + endoscopic ultrasound**; somatostatin-receptor scintigraphy or **68Ga-DOTATATE PET**

blocks.text: Age cut-offs differ. For dyspepsia both Davidson and Kumar use **55**. For reflux without alarm features, Davidson investigates from **50–55**, while Kumar treats patients **under 45** without tests.

sections.title: Complications of PUD: perforation, obstruction, penetration

blocks.title: Perforation
items: More common with **DU** than GU, usually **anterior wall** ulcers; NSAIDs often involved; may be the **first** sign of ulcer
Sudden severe upper abdominal pain that quickly becomes **generalised**; **shoulder-tip pain** (diaphragmatic irritation)
Shallow breathing, shock, abdomen held still with **board-like rigidity**, absent bowel sounds, reduced liver dullness
A deceptive lull after some hours, then generalised peritonitis
**Erect chest X-ray** shows free gas under the diaphragm in at least **50%**; if not, a **water-soluble contrast** study shows the leak
Mortality about **25%** (old, comorbid patients); signs may be masked by glucocorticoids

blocks.note: Look at: free air beneath both hemidiaphragms (pneumoperitoneum) on chest radiographs of a perforated duodenal ulcer.

blocks.title: Treating perforation
items: Resuscitate, then **surgery**: simple closure (oversew/patch), or pyloroplasty if large; rarely a Polya gastrectomy
Usually done laparoscopically, with drainage
Very sick or elderly patients: occasionally **conservative** (nasogastric suction, IV fluids, antibiotics)
Afterwards: treat H. pylori if present and avoid NSAIDs

blocks.title: Gastric outlet obstruction
items: Causes (Box 21.39): fibrotic pyloric stenosis from DU, **oedema** from a pyloric-channel or duodenal ulcer, antral carcinoma, adult hypertrophic pyloric stenosis
Large-volume vomiting containing food eaten **24 h or more** earlier; nausea, distension, wasting, dehydration
**Succussion splash** 4 h or more after food; **visible gastric peristalsis** is diagnostic
Bloods: **hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis** with high bicarbonate and urea
**Paradoxical aciduria**: the kidney conserves Na+ in exchange for H+

blocks.title: Managing gastric outlet obstruction
rows: Empty the stomach with a **wide-bore nasogastric tube** before endoscopy
IV isotonic saline; severe cases may need ≥ 4 L and 80 mmol potassium in 24 h
**Endoscopic balloon dilatation** or surgery (partial gastrectomy after about 7 days of NG aspiration)

blocks.text: Commonest cause of outlet obstruction: Davidson says a **pyloric-region ulcer**; Kumar says ulcer and gastric cancer are now uncommon, with **Crohn’s** or **pancreatic carcinoma** compression more common, and KC Essentials names **carcinoma**. Follow Davidson, but always exclude cancer. Kumar: about 70% are managed without surgery.

blocks.title: Penetration and post-surgical problems
items: **Posterior penetration** into the pancreas: pain becomes constant, severe and radiates to the back, stops responding to antisecretory drugs; amylase may rise; CT confirms
After gastric surgery: **dumping** (flushing, palpitations, sweating, tachycardia, hypotension, diarrhoea after meals: avoid large carbohydrate meals), bile-reflux gastropathy, diarrhoea, weight loss
Long-term: **anaemia** (iron deficiency commonest; B12 and folate less often), osteoporosis/osteomalacia, gastric remnant cancer

sections.title: Bleeding peptic ulcer: PUD as an acute emergency

blocks.title: Causes of acute upper GI bleeding (Fig. 21.19)
Clinical picture
items: Commonest GI emergency; in-hospital mortality about **10%**; about **85%** stop bleeding by themselves within 48 h
Haematemesis: red with clots if brisk, **coffee grounds** if slower; **melaena** = black tarry stool
A massive upper GI bleed can give fresh or maroon blood per rectum, almost always with **shock**
Syncope reflects hypovolaemia; Hb may be normal early until haemodilution
**Urea rises** because digested blood is absorbed; high urea with normal creatinine implies a **major bleed**

blocks.title: Risk scores
rows: Urea, Hb, systolic BP, pulse ≥ 100, melaena, syncope, liver disease, cardiac failure
Score 0–1 may allow discharge with outpatient endoscopy
Adds endoscopic diagnosis and stigmata of recent haemorrhage

blocks.title: Emergency management (Davidson’s sequence)
items: 1. **IV access** with large-bore cannula(s)
2. Assess circulation (tachycardia, hypotension, oliguria), signs of liver disease and comorbidity
3. Bloods: FBC, U&E, LFT, prothrombin time; **cross-match at least 2 units**
4. **Resuscitate** with IV crystalloid; transfuse when actively bleeding with hypotension and tachycardia
5. **Oxygen** if shocked
6. **Endoscopy after resuscitation, ideally within 24 h** (diagnostic in about 80%)
7. Hourly pulse, BP and urine output
8. Surgery if needed (below)
9. Stop NSAIDs; test for and eradicate H. pylori, then **confirm eradication**

blocks.title: Endoscopic and drug therapy
items: High-risk stigmata: **active bleeding, visible vessel, adherent clot**
**Dual therapy**: injection of dilute adrenaline **plus** a thermal (heater probe) or mechanical (clips) method
Haemostatic powder spray as rescue when standard therapy fails
Then **IV PPI**: omeprazole 80 mg bolus, then 8 mg/h for **72 h**; lowers rebleeding and need for surgery

blocks.note: Look at: an actively bleeding duodenal ulcer, and the same ulcer after adrenaline injection plus heater probe (dual therapy).

blocks.title: When to operate
items: Endoscopic haemostasis **fails** to stop active bleeding
Rebleeding **once** in an elderly or frail patient, or **twice** in a younger, fit patient
**Angiographic embolisation** is an effective alternative in frail patients
DU: **under-running** ± pyloroplasty; GU: under-running with biopsy, local excision or partial gastrectomy

blocks.text: Blatchford cut-off: Davidson calls **≤ 2** very low risk; Zero to Finals treats any score **> 0** as high risk. Use Davidson’s figure in exams.

PPI **before** endoscopy is disputed: Zero to Finals notes NICE advises against it, while Kumar’s box gives IV PPI at presentation. The use all sources agree on is IV PPI **after endoscopic therapy** for high-risk stigmata.

sections.title: Complications of GORD: oesophagitis, Barrett’s, stricture

blocks.text: **Oesophagitis** ranges from mild redness to bleeding ulceration and stricture, yet endoscopy can be normal; symptoms correlate poorly with endoscopic and histological findings. Grade it with the **Los Angeles** system.

blocks.note: Look at: severe reflux oesophagitis with near-circumferential superficial ulceration extending up the oesophagus.

blocks.title: Barrett’s oesophagus
rows: Pre-malignant: lower-oesophageal squamous epithelium replaced by **columnar** mucosa (columnar-lined oesophagus), ± intestinal metaplasia; an adaptation to chronic reflux
About **10%** of patients scoped for reflux
Male (especially white), **obesity** (central obesity about 4.3-fold), age > 50; weak link with smoking, none with alcohol
Columnar lining **> 1 cm** above the proximal gastric folds on biopsy; multiple systematic biopsies; **Prague C & M** lengths

blocks.title: Barrett’s surveillance and treatment (Davidson)
rows: **Endoscopic resection** of visible lesions + **radiofrequency ablation**, or oesophagectomy; specialist MDT

blocks.text: Neither strong acid suppression nor anti-reflux surgery makes Barrett’s regress or stops progression: treat only symptoms and complications. Ablation is for **dysplasia**, not non-dysplastic Barrett’s.

Definitions and risk figures vary: British guidance no longer requires intestinal metaplasia, American guidance does (Kumar). Zero to Finals quotes a 3–5% lifetime cancer risk; Davidson gives 0.1–0.5% per year. Quote Davidson.

blocks.title: Benign peptic stricture
items: Fibrous stricture after long-standing oesophagitis, mainly in the **elderly** with poor peristalsis
Slowly progressive dysphagia, **solids worse than liquids**; a meat bolus can cause complete obstruction
Heartburn history is common but **not invariable**
Endoscopy with **biopsy to exclude cancer**, then balloon dilatation or bougie
Then **long-term full-dose PPI** to prevent recurrence; chew well, check dentition

blocks.title: Other complications
items: **Iron-deficiency anaemia** from occult bleeding, often from erosions in the neck of a large hernia (**Cameron lesions**); still look for colorectal cancer
**Gastric volvulus** in a large intrathoracic hernia: severe chest pain, vomiting, dysphagia; CXR shows a gas bubble in the chest; NG decompression, then usually surgery
Aspiration: chronic cough, asthma, **recurrent pneumonia** (consider occult reflux in older people)
Oesophageal ulcer with bleeding; laryngitis; dental enamel erosion

blocks.text: Once the lower oesophagus becomes columnar (Barrett’s), reflux symptoms often **improve**, because columnar mucosa is less acid-sensitive. Absent heartburn does not exclude Barrett’s.

blocks.note: Look at: tongues of salmon-pink columnar mucosa extending up above the oesophago-gastric junction (Barrett’s oesophagus).

blocks.text: Aims: relieve symptoms, heal the ulcer, prevent relapse. **H. pylori eradication is the cornerstone**: every H. pylori-positive ulcer patient is offered it, and it usually removes the need for long-term acid suppression. General measures: stop smoking, avoid aspirin and NSAIDs; moderate alcohol is fine and no special diet is needed.

blocks.title: Eradication regimens (Davidson)
rows: **PPI + two of amoxicillin, clarithromycin, metronidazole**, at least 7 days
High-dose twice-daily PPI and 10–14 days improve success; 80–90% eradication
**Bismuth quadruple**: PPI + bismuth subcitrate + metronidazole + tetracycline, 10–14 days
Sensitivity-guided third course, **levofloxacin rescue** (with PPI + clarithromycin), or long-term acid suppression
Amoxicillin resistance rare; metronidazole > 50% in some countries; clarithromycin 20–40%

blocks.title: Examinable doses and side-effects
items: Triple (KC Essentials, 14 days): omeprazole 20 mg + clarithromycin 500 mg + amoxicillin 1 g **or** metronidazole 400 mg, all twice daily
Quadruple (Kumar, 14 days): bismuth chelate 120 mg four times daily, metronidazole 400 mg three times daily, tetracycline 500 mg four times daily, PPI 20–40 mg twice daily
Side-effects: diarrhoea in 30–50% (C. difficile possible); metronidazole + alcohol → flushing and vomiting; nausea, cramps, headache, rash

blocks.title: Checking the result
items: Confirm eradication with a **urea breath test or faecal antigen** (off PPI), not serology
Uncomplicated DU: judge by symptoms; test if symptoms persist
After **bleeding or perforation**: always test, about **6 weeks** after treatment ends
**Gastric ulcer**: repeat endoscopy (Kumar: about 6 weeks) to confirm healing and exclude cancer

blocks.title: NSAID-associated ulcer
items: **Stop the NSAID**, give a **PPI**, and eradicate H. pylori if present
If an NSAID is essential: lowest dose, a COX-2-selective drug if no cardiovascular risk, plus **PPI** or **misoprostol** (800 µg/day) cover in high-risk patients
PPIs are better tolerated than misoprostol, which causes diarrhoea
Patients starting long-term NSAIDs who are H. pylori-positive should be eradicated first

blocks.title: Indications for ulcer surgery (Box 21.37)
rows: Gastric outflow obstruction; ulcer persisting despite adequate medical therapy; recurrent ulcer after gastric surgery
**Partial gastrectomy (Billroth I)**, removing the ulcer so an underlying cancer is excluded

blocks.title: Zollinger–Ellison syndrome
items: About 30% of small, single tumours can be **resected**
Otherwise **continuous PPI at double the usual dose**; octreotide can lower gastrin
Screen every patient for **MEN 1**; 5-year survival 60–75%

blocks.text: Definite indications for eradication include peptic ulcer, MALT lymphoma, family history of gastric cancer, long-term NSAID or low-dose aspirin users and PPI use for more than a year. **GORD is not an indication.**

First-line choice differs by book. Davidson: PPI + two antibiotics unless clarithromycin resistance exceeds 15%. Kumar and Washington: **bismuth quadruple** is increasingly first line. Durations vary too (7 days in Zero to Finals, 14 days in KC Essentials).

blocks.title: Step-down approach (Fig. 21.30)
items: **Lifestyle**: lose weight, avoid trigger foods, raise the bed head for night symptoms, avoid late meals, stop smoking, cut alcohol
**Antacids / alginates** for mild symptoms
**Full-dose PPI** (e.g. omeprazole 20–40 mg daily for 4–8 weeks)
Good response: **step down** to the lowest effective maintenance PPI, an H2-receptor antagonist or antacids
Poor response: reconsider the diagnosis, do **pH monitoring**, and if positive consider **fundoplication**

blocks.title: Drug classes
rows: Forms a raft over gastric contents
10 mL three times daily; magnesium salts loosen, aluminium salts constipate; separate other drugs by about 1 h; watch sodium load
Relieves symptoms but **does not heal oesophagitis**; less effective than PPIs; cimetidine inhibits cytochrome P450 (warfarin, phenytoin, theophylline)
Inhibits H+/K+-ATPase; cuts acid by up to 90%
Drug of choice for all but mild GORD; about 60% symptom-free after 4 weeks once daily; severe cases may need twice daily
Metoclopramide/domperidone of limited value; domperidone has cardiac risks
GABA-B agonist that blocks transient LOS relaxations
Prototype reflux inhibitor (Washington); cuts reflux events, but central side-effects limit use

blocks.title: PPI doses and duration
items: Omeprazole in GORD: 20–40 mg daily for 4–8 weeks, then 10–20 mg daily to maintain
Lansoprazole: 30 mg daily for 4–8 weeks; maintenance 15–30 mg daily
After 8–12 weeks, step down to the lowest dose that controls symptoms; relapse after stopping is common

blocks.title: Long-term PPI adverse effects
items: Less absorption of **iron, B12 and magnesium**
**Osteoporosis and fractures** (odds ratio 1.2–1.5)
Enteric infection: **Salmonella, Campylobacter**, possibly **C. difficile**
Faster H. pylori-related atrophy, so **eradicate H. pylori if PPI is needed > 1 year**
Rarely acute kidney injury
Omeprazole and esomeprazole inhibit **CYP2C19**, reducing activation of clopidogrel

blocks.title: Anti-reflux surgery (laparoscopic Nissen fundoplication)
items: For: failed medical therapy, unwillingness to take lifelong PPI, or **severe regurgitation**
Needs **documented acid reflux** on pH testing; over 90% satisfied at 5 years
**Never operate for a hiatus hernia alone**; poor candidates are those with dysmotility, no PPI response or functional bowel disease
Complications: dysphagia, inability to belch or vomit, **gas-bloat syndrome**, flatulence, diarrhoea

blocks.text: **H. pylori eradication has no therapeutic role in GORD**, and H2-receptor antagonists do not heal oesophagitis. Use a PPI to heal erosive disease.

cards.front: Ulcer versus erosion: what is the histological difference?
cards.back: An ulcer penetrates the **muscularis mucosae**; an erosion does not.

cards.front: Share of duodenal and gastric ulcer patients carrying H. pylori (Davidson)?
cards.back: About **90%** of DU and **70%** of GU; most remaining GUs are NSAID-related.

cards.front: Two most important risk factors for an NSAID-induced ulcer?
cards.back: **Age > 60** and a **past history of peptic ulcer** (Box 24.31).

cards.front: Zollinger–Ellison syndrome: triad and MEN 1 link?
cards.back: Severe peptic ulceration + acid hypersecretion + gastrin-secreting tumour of pancreas/duodenum; **20–60%** have MEN 1.

cards.front: Which mechanism causes most reflux episodes in GORD?
cards.back: **Transient LOS relaxations** (not triggered by swallowing), about two-thirds of GORD reflux.

cards.front: Which hiatus hernia risks volvulus or strangulation, and what happens to the LOS?
cards.back: **Rolling (para-oesophageal)**: fundus beside the oesophagus; the LOS stays below the diaphragm and competent.

cards.front: Alarm features in dyspepsia (Box 21.15)?
cards.back: Anaemia, weight loss, dysphagia, vomiting, haematemesis or melaena, an abdominal mass (plus new dyspepsia over 55).

cards.front: Classic effect of eating on gastric versus duodenal ulcer pain?
cards.back: Eating tends to **worsen GU** pain and **ease DU** pain (classic but unreliable).

cards.front: How long off PPIs and antibiotics before a breath or stool H. pylori test?
cards.back: PPIs **2 weeks**, antibiotics **4 weeks**; H2-receptor antagonists can continue.

cards.front: 24-hour pH study: diagnostic threshold for reflux disease?
cards.back: Oesophageal pH **< 4 for more than 6–7%** of the recording.

cards.front: Los Angeles grade D oesophagitis?
cards.back: Mucosal breaks involving **≥ 75%** of the oesophageal circumference.

cards.front: Secretin test result in gastrinoma?
cards.back: A **paradoxical, marked rise** in serum gastrin (normally no change or a slight fall).

cards.front: Typical biochemistry in gastric outlet obstruction?
cards.back: **Hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis**, raised urea, with **paradoxical aciduria**.

cards.front: Perforated ulcer: yield of erect CXR, next test if negative, mortality?
cards.back: Free gas in **≥ 50%**; if absent use a **water-soluble contrast** study; mortality about **25%**.

cards.front: Components of the Blatchford score and Davidson’s low-risk cut-off?
cards.back: Urea, Hb, systolic BP, pulse, melaena, syncope, liver disease, cardiac failure; **≤ 2** = very low risk.

cards.front: IV PPI regimen after endoscopic therapy of a bleeding ulcer?
cards.back: Omeprazole **80 mg bolus, then 8 mg/h for 72 h**.

cards.front: When is surgery indicated for a bleeding ulcer (Davidson)?
cards.back: Failed endoscopic haemostasis, or rebleeding **once** if elderly/frail or **twice** if young and fit; embolisation is an alternative in the frail.

cards.front: Barrett’s oesophagus: relative and absolute cancer risk?
cards.back: Relative risk **40–120-fold**; absolute **0.1–0.5% per year**.

cards.front: Barrett’s surveillance intervals without dysplasia (Davidson)?
cards.back: **3–5 yearly** if < 3 cm; **2–3 yearly** if > 3 cm; low-grade dysplasia every 6 months.

cards.front: Management of a benign peptic stricture?
cards.back: Biopsy to exclude cancer, **endoscopic dilatation**, then **long-term full-dose PPI**.

cards.front: Davidson’s first-line H. pylori eradication and when to switch?
cards.back: PPI + two of amoxicillin/clarithromycin/metronidazole ≥ 7 days; use **bismuth quadruple** where clarithromycin resistance > 15%.

cards.front: Operation for a chronic non-healing gastric ulcer?
cards.back: **Partial gastrectomy (Billroth I)**, which removes the ulcer and excludes cancer.

cards.front: H2-receptor antagonist versus PPI in oesophagitis?
cards.back: H2RAs relieve symptoms but **do not heal oesophagitis**; PPIs heal it and are drugs of choice.

cards.front: Long-term PPI adverse effects?
cards.back: Low iron, B12, magnesium; fractures (OR 1.2–1.5); Salmonella, Campylobacter, possibly C. difficile; reduced clopidogrel activation (omeprazole).

cards.front: Indications for laparoscopic fundoplication?
cards.back: PPI failure, unwilling to take lifelong PPI, severe regurgitation, **with acid reflux proven on pH study**; never for hernia alone.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man has a duodenal ulcer. Antral biopsies show chronic active gastritis with H. pylori. His basal and stimulated acid outputs are high.
questions.leadIn: Which mechanism best links his infection to the duodenal ulcer?
options: Loss of antral somatostatin causing raised gastrin release
Direct invasion of normal duodenal villous epithelium
questions.explanation: Antral-predominant H. pylori gastritis depletes D-cell somatostatin, so G cells release more gastrin and acid output rises. The duodenal acid load induces gastric metaplasia, which the organism then colonises, causing duodenitis and ulceration.
whyNot: Corpus-predominant gastritis lowers acid and predisposes to gastric ulcer and cancer, not to the high acid output seen here.
Autoimmune gastritis destroys parietal cells and causes achlorhydria and pernicious anaemia.
This is how NSAIDs injure mucosa, not H. pylori.
H. pylori colonises only gastric-type epithelium; in the duodenum it is found only on patches of gastric metaplasia.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man is about to start long-term diclofenac for hip osteoarthritis. He asks which part of his history matters most for ulcer risk.
questions.leadIn: Which factor does Davidson rank among the most important risks for an NSAID-induced ulcer?
options: Two cups of coffee a day
questions.explanation: Box 24.31 marks **age over 60** and a **past peptic ulcer** as the most important risks; others are prior NSAID adverse events, glucocorticoid co-therapy, high-dose or multiple NSAIDs and high-risk NSAIDs.
whyNot: Coffee has not been shown to raise peptic ulcer risk.
Spicy food has not been shown to raise peptic ulcer risk.
Psychological stress has not been shown to raise peptic ulcer risk.
Davidson states moderate alcohol is not harmful in ulcer disease.

questions.stem: A 41-year-old woman has typical post-prandial heartburn. Manometry shows normal resting lower oesophageal sphincter pressure, and she has no hiatus hernia.
questions.leadIn: Which mechanism most likely explains her reflux episodes?
questions.explanation: Transient LOS relaxations occur independently of swallowing, especially after meals. They cause almost all reflux in healthy people and about two-thirds of reflux in GORD, and they occur even when basal tone is normal.
whyNot: Her resting sphincter pressure is normal, so a permanently hypotonic LOS does not fit.
Imaging shows no hernia; reflux can occur without one.
It contributes in some patients but does not explain reflux on its own here.
Bile adds to mucosal injury but does not explain why the sphincter lets contents reflux.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old woman has episodes of severe lower chest pain and retching. Barium meal shows the gastric fundus lying in the chest beside the oesophagus, with the gastro-oesophageal junction below the diaphragm.
questions.leadIn: Which complication is this type of hernia most associated with?
questions.explanation: This is a **rolling (para-oesophageal)** hernia: the junction stays below the diaphragm and the sphincter remains competent, so reflux is not the main problem; the danger is **volvulus or strangulation**.
whyNot: Barrett’s is a reflux complication; a rolling hernia leaves the sphincter competent.
Peptic stricture follows long-standing reflux oesophagitis, typical of sliding hernias.
Reflux oesophagitis goes with an incompetent sphincter, as in sliding hernias.
Cameron lesions occur at the neck of large hernias but this vignette points to an acute mechanical complication.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old man has months of burning upper abdominal pain that wakes him at 2 a.m. and settles with antacids or food. Asked where it hurts, he points with one finger to his epigastrium. He has no weight loss or vomiting.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Pointing with one finger to the epigastrium strongly suggests peptic ulcer, and nocturnal hunger pain eased by food or antacids is the classic (if unreliable) duodenal pattern.
whyNot: He is young with no alarm features such as weight loss, anaemia or vomiting.
Functional dyspepsia typically causes morning nausea, satiety and bloating rather than nocturnal pain relieved by food.
GORD gives retrosternal burning and regurgitation provoked by bending or lying.
Gallstones are rarely responsible for dyspeptic symptoms.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man has burning central chest pain, worse when he bends to tie his shoes or lies flat after dinner. ECG and troponin are normal.
questions.leadIn: Which feature would most strongly favour reflux over myocardial ischaemia?
questions.explanation: Reflux pain is burning, provoked by bending, stooping or lying down, seldom radiates to the arms and is relieved by antacids. A cardiac cause must still be excluded first.
whyNot: Radiation to the neck or left arm is typical of ischaemic pain.
Exertional pain points to ischaemia.
Dyspnoea accompanies ischaemic pain.
Gripping or crushing pain is the ischaemic pattern.

questions.stem: A 46-year-old woman completed eradication therapy for H. pylori after a bleeding duodenal ulcer. She has been off all acid-suppressing drugs and antibiotics for 6 weeks.
questions.leadIn: Which test is best to confirm eradication?
options: Rapid urease test on biopsies taken while on a PPI
questions.explanation: After a complicated ulcer, eradication must be proven, using a breath or stool antigen test done off PPI. The urea breath test is highly sensitive and specific.
whyNot: IgG titres fall slowly after cure, so serology cannot confirm eradication.
Salivary antibody tests are less accurate than serology and share its limitation.
PPIs cause false-negative urease tests, and endoscopy is unnecessary for this purpose.
Culture is slow, insensitive and invasive; it is kept for defining antibiotic sensitivities.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old man with iron-deficiency anaemia undergoes endoscopy. A 2 cm ulcer on the lesser curve looks benign, with smooth regular edges.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Multiple biopsies from rim and base, then repeat endoscopy to confirm healing
No biopsy, because the ulcer looks benign
Serum gastrin before any further action
questions.explanation: Benign and malignant gastric ulcers can look identical, so every GU is biopsied (several samples) and followed endoscopically until healed.
whyNot: Appearance cannot exclude malignancy; GU must always be biopsied.
Barium misses small lesions and cannot give histology.
Gastrin is for suspected Zollinger–Ellison syndrome (multiple, unusual-site, refractory ulcers), not a single GU.
CT does not replace tissue diagnosis.

questions.stem: A 61-year-old man known to have had duodenal ulcers for years has vomited large volumes for a week, including food he ate the previous day. A succussion splash is present 5 hours after his last drink.
questions.leadIn: Which blood result pattern is expected?
options: Low chloride, low potassium, high bicarbonate
High chloride, normal anion gap, low bicarbonate
Normal chloride, normal potassium, normal bicarbonate
questions.explanation: Loss of acidic gastric juice gives a **hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis** with raised bicarbonate and urea; the urine may be paradoxically acidic as the kidney retains sodium in exchange for H+.
whyNot: A hyperchloraemic acidosis follows bicarbonate loss (e.g. diarrhoea), not loss of gastric acid.
A high anion gap acidosis implies added acid (e.g. ketones, lactate).
Vomiting causes potassium loss and alkalosis.
A week of copious vomiting will disturb electrolytes.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old woman taking naproxen develops sudden severe epigastric pain that spreads over the whole abdomen within an hour. She has right shoulder-tip pain, a rigid silent abdomen and is tachycardic.
questions.leadIn: Which is the most appropriate first imaging test?
questions.explanation: The picture is a perforated peptic ulcer. An **erect CXR** shows free gas under the diaphragm in at least half of cases; if it is negative, a **water-soluble** contrast study confirms the leak.
whyNot: Davidson’s pathway for suspected perforation is imaging: an erect CXR for free gas, then a water-soluble contrast study if needed; endoscopy is not part of it.
If contrast is needed, a water-soluble agent is used, not barium.
Ultrasound is not in Davidson’s pathway; free gas is sought first on an erect CXR, then a leak on water-soluble contrast.
Testing for H. pylori comes after surgical treatment, not during the acute diagnosis.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man vomited once after a night of heavy drinking; the vomit had a few streaks of blood. Pulse 78, BP 128/76, Hb 148 g/L, urea normal. No melaena, syncope, liver or heart disease.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate management?
options: Transfuse two units of red cells
questions.explanation: His Glasgow-Blatchford score is 0 (normal urea, Hb ≥ 130 g/L, systolic BP > 109, pulse < 100, no melaena, syncope, liver or cardiac disease). Davidson regards a score of 2 or less as very low risk, and his pre-endoscopy Rockall score is also 0; Kumar notes that pre-endoscopy Rockall scores of 0–1 may allow discharge with outpatient endoscopy.
whyNot: Urgent endoscopy is for shocked patients or high-risk scores.
The high-dose IV PPI regimen is for ulcers with high-risk stigmata after endoscopic therapy.
He is haemodynamically stable with a normal Hb.
Terlipressin is for suspected variceal bleeding; nothing suggests liver disease.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man has endoscopy for melaena. A duodenal ulcer with a visible vessel is treated with adrenaline injection and clips.
questions.leadIn: Which drug treatment should follow?
options: IV omeprazole 80 mg bolus then 8 mg/h for 72 hours
questions.explanation: After endoscopic haemostasis of an ulcer with high-risk stigmata, a high-dose IV PPI for 72 hours reduces rebleeding and the need for surgery.
whyNot: The cited post-haemostasis treatment is high-dose IV PPI for 72 hours; PPIs are more effective than H2-receptor antagonists (KC Essentials).
Terlipressin is used when variceal bleeding is suspected.
Octreotide is used to lower gastrin in gastrinoma, not to prevent ulcer rebleeding.
Tranexamic acid showed a mortality signal in meta-analysis but did not reduce rebleeding or surgery.

questions.stem: A 57-year-old man with long-standing reflux has a 5 cm segment of columnar-lined oesophagus. Biopsies show intestinal metaplasia without dysplasia.
questions.leadIn: According to Davidson, how often should he have surveillance endoscopy?
questions.explanation: For non-dysplastic Barrett’s with intestinal metaplasia, Davidson advises 3–5-yearly endoscopy for segments under 3 cm and **2–3-yearly** for segments over 3 cm. His segment is 5 cm.
whyNot: Six-monthly endoscopy is for low-grade dysplasia.
Annual endoscopy is not one of Davidson’s intervals.
This interval applies to segments shorter than 3 cm.
Barrett’s carries a 0.1–0.5% yearly cancer risk; surveillance is recommended.

questions.stem: A 78-year-old woman has dysphagia for solids that has slowly worsened over 8 months. She has had heartburn for years. Endoscopy shows a smooth short narrowing above the gastro-oesophageal junction with oesophagitis; biopsies are benign.
questions.leadIn: What is the best management?
options: Endoscopic dilatation, then long-term full-dose PPI
questions.explanation: This is a benign peptic stricture. After biopsy excludes cancer, it is dilated endoscopically and then a full-dose PPI is continued long term to prevent recurrence.
whyNot: Oesophagectomy is an option for high-grade dysplasia or cancer, not a benign stricture.
Eradication has no therapeutic value in reflux disease.
Swallowed steroid treats eosinophilic oesophagitis.
H2RAs do not heal oesophagitis and are inadequate to prevent stricture recurrence.

questions.stem: A 37-year-old woman has an H. pylori-positive duodenal ulcer. Local clarithromycin resistance is 25%. She has never had eradication therapy.
questions.leadIn: Which first-line regimen is most appropriate?
options: PPI + bismuth subcitrate + metronidazole + tetracycline for 10–14 days
questions.explanation: Where clarithromycin resistance exceeds 15%, Davidson recommends bismuth-based quadruple therapy (OBMT) for 10–14 days.
whyNot: Clarithromycin triple therapy is undermined by resistance above 15%.
Levofloxacin regimens are rescue therapy after two failures.
Acid suppression alone heals but does not prevent relapse; eradication is the cornerstone.
Eradication regimens always pair antibiotics with powerful acid suppression.

questions.stem: A 71-year-old man with rheumatoid arthritis had a bleeding gastric ulcer last year. He is H. pylori negative and has no cardiovascular disease. His rheumatologist says an NSAID is essential.
questions.leadIn: What is the best strategy to continue the NSAID?
options: Lowest-dose COX-2-selective drug with PPI cover
Standard NSAID with an antacid as needed
Standard NSAID with standard-dose H2-receptor antagonist
questions.explanation: In a high-risk patient (previous ulcer complication, older age) who must take an NSAID, use the lowest dose, a COX-2 agent if there is no cardiovascular risk, and protective PPI (or misoprostol) cover.
whyNot: Antacids are only adjuncts for symptom relief and are not recommended as primary therapy.
Davidson states that standard-dose H2-receptor antagonists do not prevent NSAID ulcers; a PPI or misoprostol is needed.
Sucralfate coats ulcers but does not block acid and is not the recommended prophylaxis.
He is high risk; prophylaxis is required.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old woman who has taken omeprazole for 9 years presents with muscle cramps and carpopedal spasm.
questions.leadIn: Which electrolyte abnormality is the most likely PPI-related cause?
questions.explanation: Long-term PPIs reduce intestinal absorption of **magnesium** (as well as iron, B12 and calcium), so low magnesium is the expected electrolyte effect; calcium malabsorption also explains the modest rise in fracture risk.
whyNot: Long-term PPI effects are deficiencies from reduced absorption (magnesium, calcium, B12, iron); a raised potassium is not among them.
Long-term PPI effects are deficiencies from reduced absorption (magnesium, calcium, B12, iron); a raised sodium is not among them.
PPIs are linked to calcium malabsorption (fracture risk), not raised calcium.
Long-term PPI effects are deficiencies from reduced absorption (magnesium, calcium, B12, iron); a raised phosphate is not among them.

questions.stem: A 33-year-old man has 3 months of typical heartburn and regurgitation. He has no dysphagia, weight loss or anaemia. Weight loss and avoiding late meals have not helped.
questions.leadIn: What is the next step?
questions.explanation: Young patients with typical symptoms and no alarm features are treated empirically. After lifestyle measures fail, a full-dose PPI is the next step, then step down.
whyNot: Endoscopy is for age over 50–55, alarm or atypical features, or suspected complications.
Eradication has no value in GORD.
Surgery is for PPI failure or intolerance with acid reflux documented on pH testing.
pH monitoring is for diagnostic uncertainty or before surgery.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old man has three ulcers in the post-bulbar duodenum and upper jejunum despite 8 weeks of standard PPI therapy. He has had watery diarrhoea for 2 months. Stool antigen is negative and he takes no NSAIDs. His brother had a parathyroid adenoma removed.
questions.leadIn: Which investigation is most likely to confirm the diagnosis?
options: Fasting serum gastrin off acid suppression
questions.explanation: Step 1: the clues are **multiple ulcers in unusual sites** (post-bulbar, jejunum), **refractory** to standard therapy, with **diarrhoea**. Step 2: H. pylori negative and no NSAIDs, so the usual causes are excluded. Step 3: a family history suggesting **MEN 1** points to a **gastrinoma (Zollinger–Ellison)**. Step 4: confirm with a grossly raised **fasting gastrin** (off acid suppression), then a secretin test if needed, then localise with CT + EUS.
whyNot: He is already stool-antigen negative; H. pylori would not explain this pattern.
Barium may show ulcers but cannot identify their cause.
Amylase helps with posterior penetration into the pancreas, not with acid hypersecretion.
Culture is for H. pylori antibiotic sensitivities.

questions.stem: An 84-year-old frail woman with heart failure had a bleeding gastric ulcer treated with adrenaline injection and heater probe yesterday and is on IV PPI. She now has fresh haematemesis, pulse 118 and BP 88/50 despite fluids.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Wait for a second rebleed before intervening
questions.explanation: Step 1: this is a **rebleed** after endoscopic therapy. Step 2: Davidson’s rule is that surgery is indicated after **one** rebleed in an **elderly or frail** patient (two in a fit younger patient). Step 3: in a frail patient, **angiographic embolisation** is an effective alternative to surgery. Resuscitation continues throughout.
whyNot: Waiting for a second rebleed applies to younger, fitter patients.
Changing the route of acid suppression does not deal with a shocked rebleed; Davidson’s next step is surgery or, in the frail, embolisation.
Terlipressin is for variceal bleeding.
Tranexamic acid did not reduce rebleeding or surgery in meta-analysis.

questions.leadIn: Match each patient below to the best option from the list. An option can fit several patients or none.
options: Free perforation into the peritoneal cavity
Pyloric oedema from an active channel ulcer
Acute haemorrhage from a duodenal ulcer

items.stem: A 59-year-old man with known duodenal ulcer has had 2 weeks of constant, severe epigastric pain boring through to his back. It no longer responds to his PPI. Serum amylase is mildly raised and CT shows the ulcer crater abutting the pancreas.
items.explanation: Constant pain radiating to the back that has stopped responding to antisecretory drugs, with a raised amylase, means the ulcer has **penetrated posteriorly into the pancreas**. CT confirms.

items.stem: A 66-year-old man has weeks of large vomits containing food from the day before, a succussion splash and a hypokalaemic alkalosis. After NG emptying, endoscopy shows a tight, scarred pylorus with no active ulcer, and 4 weeks of PPI have not helped.
items.explanation: Step 1: the features are gastric outlet obstruction. Step 2: there is no active ulcer or oedema, PPI failed and the pylorus is scarred, so this is **fibrotic stenosis**, treated with balloon dilatation or surgery rather than PPI.

items.stem: A 55-year-old woman had a partial gastrectomy years ago. Within 30 minutes of meals she gets flushing, palpitations, sweating, abdominal discomfort and loose stools, worse after sugary food.
items.explanation: Rapid gastric emptying of hypertonic contents draws fluid into the small bowel and triggers vasomotor reflexes: **dumping**. Avoid large carbohydrate-rich meals.

questions.theme: Causes of peptic ulceration and mucosal injury
questions.leadIn: Match each patient below to the best option from the list. An option can fit several patients or none.
options: H. pylori corpus-predominant gastritis with atrophy
Ectopic gastric mucosa in a Meckel’s diverticulum

items.stem: A 32-year-old man has a duodenal cap ulcer. A biopsy urease test is positive. He takes no medicines. Gastric acid output is high.
items.explanation: Duodenal ulcer with H. pylori and high acid output fits **antral-predominant gastritis**: low somatostatin, high gastrin, acid hypersecretion.

items.stem: A 47-year-old woman has ulcers in the jejunum and lower oesophagus and watery diarrhoea. She is H. pylori negative and takes no NSAIDs. Her father had parathyroid surgery and a pituitary tumour.
items.explanation: Two steps: unusual-site, multiple ulcers with diarrhoea suggest gastrinoma; the family history suggests **MEN 1**, present in 20–60% of Zollinger–Ellison cases.

items.stem: A 76-year-old woman takes ibuprofen daily for knee osteoarthritis. Endoscopy shows an antral gastric ulcer; biopsies are benign and H. pylori tests are negative.
items.explanation: Most gastric ulcers not caused by H. pylori are due to **NSAIDs**, which block cyclo-oxygenase and deplete protective prostaglandins.

items.stem: A 55-year-old man is on day 10 in intensive care after extensive burns. He has a small haematemesis. Endoscopy shows multiple superficial gastric erosions.
items.explanation: Severe physiological stress such as burns causes acute erosive, haemorrhagic gastritis (stress or Curling ulcers).

questions.leadIn: Match each patient below to the best option from the list. An option can fit several patients or none.
options: Rapid urease (CLO) test on antral biopsy
Culture of gastric biopsy with sensitivities

items.stem: A 36-year-old woman with typical heartburn has a normal endoscopy and only a partial PPI response. She is being considered for fundoplication.
items.explanation: Acid reflux must be **documented on pH testing** before anti-reflux surgery; pH < 4 for over 6–7% of the time is diagnostic.

items.stem: A 61-year-old man has new dyspepsia and has lost 5 kg in 2 months.
items.explanation: New dyspepsia over 55 with an alarm feature (weight loss) needs **urgent endoscopy**, not a test-and-treat approach.

items.stem: A 48-year-old woman still has H. pylori after two different eradication courses, despite good adherence. A third course is planned.
items.explanation: After two failures, a third attempt should be **guided by antibiotic sensitivities**, which only culture provides.

items.stem: A 72-year-old man has sudden severe epigastric pain and generalised guarding. An erect chest X-ray shows no free gas, but perforation is still suspected.
items.explanation: Two steps: free gas is seen in only about half of perforations, so a negative CXR does not exclude it; a **water-soluble contrast** study confirms a leak.

questions.leadIn: Match each patient below to the best option from the list. An option can fit several patients or none.
options: Cameron erosions in a hiatus hernia

items.stem: An 81-year-old woman with a large hiatus hernia has iron-deficiency anaemia. Colonoscopy is normal. Endoscopy shows linear erosions where the hernia passes through the diaphragm.
items.explanation: Two steps: colorectal cancer has been excluded first, as Davidson insists; erosions in the neck of the hernia sac are **Cameron lesions**, causing occult blood loss.

items.stem: A 79-year-old man has had three right lower lobe pneumonias in a year, with nocturnal coughing and regurgitation.
items.explanation: In older people with recurrent pneumonia, consider **aspiration** from occult reflux.

items.stem: A 60-year-old obese man with years of reflux has salmon-pink tongues of mucosa extending 4 cm above the gastro-oesophageal junction. Biopsies show intestinal metaplasia with no dysplasia.
items.explanation: Columnar mucosa above the gastric folds = **Barrett’s**; no dysplasia, so surveillance (2–3 yearly for > 3 cm).

items.stem: A 70-year-old woman with a massive intrathoracic hiatus hernia has sudden severe chest pain, vomiting and dysphagia. CXR shows a gas bubble in the chest.
items.explanation: A large intrathoracic hernia that twists causes **gastric volvulus**; managed with NG decompression and then usually surgery.

questions.theme: Drug and procedural treatment of acid-related disease
questions.leadIn: Match each patient below to the best option from the list. An option can fit several patients or none.
options: Lifestyle advice with alginate–antacid as needed
Maintenance PPI at the lowest effective dose
Stop the NSAID and give a PPI
Endoscopic balloon dilatation with long-term PPI

items.stem: A 52-year-old woman has a gastrinoma with liver metastases, so resection is not possible. She has refractory ulcers and diarrhoea.
items.explanation: Unresectable Zollinger–Ellison syndrome is controlled with **continuous PPI at double the normal dose** (octreotide may help).

items.stem: A 44-year-old man’s LA grade C oesophagitis healed on 8 weeks of PPI, but heartburn returned within a month of stopping it.
items.explanation: Relapse after stopping is common; step down to the **lowest effective maintenance PPI** dose.

items.stem: A 29-year-old man has an H. pylori-positive duodenal ulcer. Local clarithromycin resistance is 8% and he has never taken a macrolide.
items.explanation: With low clarithromycin resistance, Davidson’s first line is **PPI + two antibiotics** (amoxicillin and clarithromycin), ideally 10–14 days.

items.stem: A 46-year-old woman has troublesome regurgitation on PPI and does not want lifelong tablets. A 24-hour pH study shows abnormal acid exposure that matches her symptoms.
items.explanation: Severe regurgitation, unwillingness to take lifelong PPI and **proven acid reflux** are indications for **laparoscopic fundoplication**.

questions.theme: Acute upper GI bleeding: next step
questions.leadIn: Match each patient below to the best option from the list. An option can fit several patients or none.
options: Adrenaline injection plus heater probe or clips
Urea breath test to confirm eradication

items.stem: A 53-year-old man has haematemesis. Endoscopy shows a duodenal ulcer with an arterial spurt from its base.
items.explanation: Active bleeding is a major stigma; treat with **dual therapy**: dilute adrenaline injection plus a thermal or mechanical method.

items.stem: A 34-year-old fit man had a bleeding duodenal ulcer treated endoscopically. He rebled on day 2 and repeat endoscopic therapy worked. On day 4 he rebleeds again and becomes shocked.
items.explanation: Two steps: a fit young patient warrants surgery after a **second** rebleed; for a duodenal ulcer this means **under-running** ± pyloroplasty.

items.stem: A 58-year-old man with spider naevi, ascites and jaundice has a large haematemesis. Endoscopy shows bleeding oesophageal varices.
items.explanation: Variceal bleeding is treated with **band ligation**; balloon tamponade and TIPSS are fallbacks.

items.stem: A 47-year-old woman recovered from a bleeding duodenal ulcer and finished H. pylori eradication 6 weeks ago. She is off PPIs.
items.explanation: After a **complicated** ulcer, eradication must be **confirmed** by breath or faecal antigen testing.

questions.leadIn: Match each patient below to the best option from the list. An option can fit several patients or none.

items.stem: A 27-year-old woman has early-morning nausea, early satiety and bloating after meals for a year. She has not lost weight. Endoscopy is normal and H. pylori is negative.
items.explanation: Chronic dyspepsia with no organic cause in a young woman, with morning symptoms and post-meal fullness, is **functional dyspepsia**.

items.stem: A 22-year-old man with asthma and eczema presents with a food bolus stuck in his oesophagus. He rarely has heartburn. Endoscopy shows mucosal rings.
items.explanation: An atopic young adult with dysphagia or bolus obstruction more than heartburn, and rings at endoscopy, suggests **eosinophilic oesophagitis**.

items.stem: A 61-year-old smoker has retrosternal tightness when walking uphill. It spreads to his neck and left arm, comes with breathlessness and settles with rest.
items.explanation: Exertional, crushing pain that radiates to neck or arm, with breathlessness, is **ischaemic**, not reflux.

items.stem: A 70-year-old woman taking diclofenac has sudden severe epigastric pain that becomes generalised, with left shoulder-tip pain and a board-like abdomen.
items.explanation: Sudden pain spreading across the abdomen, shoulder-tip pain and rigidity in an NSAID user = **perforated ulcer**.

questions.stem: A 39-year-old man with heartburn has a normal endoscopy. A 24-hour oesophageal pH study is performed.
questions.leadIn: Which result is diagnostic of reflux disease according to Davidson?
options: pH below 4 for more than 6–7% of the recording
pH below 2 for more than 1% of the recording
pH above 7 for more than 10% of the recording
pH below 4 for more than half the recording
Any single episode of pH below 4
questions.explanation: Davidson defines reflux disease as oesophageal pH < 4 for more than 6–7% of the study time. Kumar adds a composite DeMeester score above 14.72.
whyNot: This is not the threshold used.
Alkaline reflux is detected by impedance, not by this criterion.
Far stricter than needed; disease is diagnosed well below this.
Occasional reflux episodes are normal.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old man in Barrett’s surveillance has high-grade dysplasia in a flat segment that contains a small nodule.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate management?
options: Endoscopic resection of the nodule plus radiofrequency ablation
Double the PPI dose and repeat endoscopy in 3–5 years
questions.explanation: For high-grade dysplasia or intramucosal cancer, Davidson offers endoscopic resection of visible lesions plus radiofrequency ablation of the rest (organ-preserving), or oesophagectomy, decided by an MDT.
whyNot: Acid suppression does not cause regression or stop progression of Barrett’s.
Anti-reflux surgery does not reverse Barrett’s or treat dysplasia.
Davidson finds no therapeutic value for H. pylori eradication in reflux disease, and it does nothing for dysplasia.
Six-monthly surveillance is for low-grade dysplasia.

questions.theme: Managing complications of peptic ulcer disease
questions.leadIn: Match each patient below to the best option from the list. An option can fit several patients or none.
options: Conservative NG suction, IV fluids and antibiotics
Wide-bore NG drainage, IV saline with potassium, then PPI

items.stem: A 45-year-old fit man has sudden generalised abdominal pain and rigidity. Erect CXR shows free gas under both hemidiaphragms.
items.explanation: Perforation in a fit patient: **resuscitate, then surgery** (simple closure, or pyloroplasty if large), followed by H. pylori treatment and NSAID avoidance.

items.stem: A 93-year-old woman with severe heart and lung disease has a perforated duodenal ulcer. She is judged unfit for an operation.
items.explanation: Very sick elderly patients may be treated **conservatively** with NG suction, IV fluids and antibiotics.

items.stem: A 63-year-old man has days of vomiting, dehydration and a hypochloraemic alkalosis. After NG emptying, endoscopy shows an active pyloric-channel ulcer with swollen surrounding mucosa.
items.explanation: Two steps: outlet obstruction first needs NG emptying and IV saline with potassium; obstruction from **oedema** around an active ulcer then settles with a PPI.

items.stem: A 58-year-old woman has a gastric ulcer that has not healed after 12 weeks of PPI, with eradication confirmed and NSAIDs stopped. Repeated biopsies are benign.
items.explanation: A chronic non-healing GU is treated by **partial gastrectomy with Billroth I** anastomosis, which also excludes hidden cancer.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man with pyloric stenosis has vomited for 10 days. Blood shows a metabolic alkalosis with low potassium and chloride, yet his urine is acidic.
questions.leadIn: What best explains the acidic urine?
options: Renal sodium retention in exchange for hydrogen ions
questions.explanation: Davidson explains **paradoxical aciduria** by enhanced renal sodium reabsorption in exchange for H+, as the volume-depleted kidney conserves sodium despite the alkalosis.
whyNot: Renal tubular acidosis causes systemic acidosis, not alkalosis.
Starvation ketosis does not explain acid urine alongside a marked alkalosis.
Compensation for metabolic alkalosis is hypoventilation, and it does not acidify urine.
Vomit from an obstructed stomach is acid, which is why bicarbonate rises.

questions.theme: Risk factors and associations in GORD and PUD
questions.leadIn: Match each patient below to the best option from the list. An option can fit several patients or none.
options: Age over 60 with previous peptic ulcer
H. pylori infection with NSAID use

items.stem: A 42-year-old woman with Raynaud’s phenomenon and tight, thickened skin over her fingers has severe heartburn and dysphagia.
items.explanation: **Systemic sclerosis** is a recognised predisposing cause of GORD.

items.stem: A 55-year-old man takes naproxen daily and has a positive stool antigen test. Meta-analysis suggests his ulcer odds are about 60 times those of an uninfected non-user.
items.explanation: H. pylori and NSAIDs are **independent and synergistic**: odds ratio about 61 for both together.

items.stem: A 73-year-old woman on omeprazole for 12 years has a fragility hip fracture and low serum magnesium.
items.explanation: **Long-term PPI** use reduces magnesium absorption and raises fracture risk (OR 1.2–1.5).

questions.stem: A student is revising the epidemiology of peptic ulcer disease from Davidson’s.
questions.leadIn: About what proportion of duodenal ulcer patients carry H. pylori?
questions.explanation: Davidson gives about **90%** for duodenal ulcer and **70%** for gastric ulcer. Kumar quotes a lower and falling 50–75% in the developed world; follow Davidson.
whyNot: 70% is Davidson’s figure for gastric ulcer.
Below both Davidson’s figure and the upper end of Kumar’s range.
30% is the share of gastric ulcers caused by NSAIDs.
Around 10% of infected people in the West develop the antral-predominant, acid-hypersecreting pattern.

ospe.identify: Endoscopy: a **clean-based duodenal ulcer** with no stigmata of recent haemorrhage (low rebleeding risk).
Endoscopy: **active arterial bleeding from a duodenal ulcer**, then haemostasis after adrenaline injection + heater probe (dual therapy).
Barium meal: **rolling (para-oesophageal) hernia** with intrathoracic stomach, and a **gastric volvulus** complicating a sliding hernia.
Endoscopy: **severe reflux oesophagitis**, near-circumferential superficial ulceration and inflammation extending up the gullet.
Endoscopy: **Barrett’s oesophagus**, salmon-pink tongues of columnar mucosa rising above the oesophago-gastric junction.
Histology: Barrett’s mucosa with **Alcian blue-staining goblet cells** (intestinal metaplasia).
Chest X-ray: **free subdiaphragmatic air** under both hemidiaphragms = pneumoperitoneum from a perforated duodenal ulcer.
Histology/SEM: **curved spiral H. pylori** organisms on gastric mucosa (modified Giemsa) and on electron microscopy.
